A_review_connect.explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to quickly review vocabulary from a unit of study and specific sentence structures children have used to express those concepts and vocabulary. Do not introduce new vocabulary or concepts. The goal is to have children apply vocabulary that they have been directly taught using sentence structures
teacher_script: [TEACHER NOTE: Ask teacher: 'What vocabulary words from your current unit have you previously taught?' and 'What sentence structures have students practiced?']
Remember boys and girls we were talking about [UNIT_TOPIC]. And we said that [KEY_CONCEPT_1] is a what? (Children should respond [EXPECTED_RESPONSE_1]).
Right, [CONCEPT_EXPLANATION]. [Additional context about the unit topic and key vocabulary]
Remember [VOCABULARY_WORD_1] [definition/explanation]. [VOCABULARY_WORD_2] [definition/explanation]. {Teacher draws children's attention to visual for [VOCABULARY_WORDS]}
[Continue with vocabulary review and connections]

Before we said every sentence needs a subject, that is the person, animal, thing, or place that we are talking about. The subject is the star of the show. Every sentence needs a subject and an action verb.

Let's play our [REVIEW_ACTIVITY] +Level: Low. I am going to tell you a sentence about [UNIT_TOPIC_EXAMPLE] and you are going to tell me the subject –the who or what [SUBJECT_TYPE] that I am talking about?

Watch me because I am going to show you how to do this. So, here's the first picture, and my sentence is [EXAMPLE_SENTENCE]. So, I am thinking What is the subject? The subject is who or what the sentence is about? In my sentence [EXAMPLE_SENTENCE], it is telling me about [SUBJECT], that is what my sentence is about. And, [SUBJECT] are the ones doing the action. They [ACTION]. So, the subject is [SUBJECT].
My turn. My sentence is [PRACTICE_SENTENCE]. {Teacher displays sentence along with the visual of the [SUBJECT] in the subject spot of the sentence}.
What is the subject? Who/What is this sentence all about? Get Ready. Go. (Children should respond, [EXPECTED_SUBJECT].)
*Let me know if you would like activity examples and/or modifications of activities based on child ability level (low, middle, high).
A_review_connect.example_output: Spotlight Sentence: Children identify subjects in sentences about unit topic. Vocabulary review using visuals and definitions. Subject-verb identification with previously learned sentence structures.
A_review_connect.reference: Form D for alternative review activities

B_model_explain_engage.explanation: The purpose of this section is to introduce and reinforce a targeted sentence structure through modeling and providing clear examples, while connecting to genre purpose and incorporating children's vocabulary associated with what they are reading and writing about in their unit of study
teacher_script: Great! So we know that a sentence needs a subject and a verb. Verbs are usually actions. But, remember we are writing [GENRE_TYPE]. Sometimes we need to tell information about our subject. Like, [TARGET_SENTENCE_EXAMPLE]. {Teacher displays the sentence}
Did the [SUBJECT] do anything? (Children should respond no).
No. we are just telling something about the [SUBJECT]'s being –or something that is about who they are as a [SUBJECT_TYPE]. So these are special verbs. They are not action verbs.
They are [TARGET_STRUCTURE]: [EXAMPLE_SENTENCE]. {Teacher circles/underlines the [TARGET_VERB]}.
I could also say [PLURAL_EXAMPLE]. {Teacher circles the word [PLURAL_VERB]}.
Why did I use [PLURAL_VERB]? (Children should respond that there is more than one.)
Right. We use the verb [PLURAL_VERB] when talking about more than one person, place, thing, or animal.
{Teacher displays the [TARGET_STRUCTURE_ELEMENTS]}. So, these [STRUCTURE_DESCRIPTION] are used to [PURPOSE_EXPLANATION].
Let me show you some more examples. {Teacher displays example sentences, calling children's attention to the purpose of the sentence and the [TARGET_STRUCTURE] used for that purpose}.
[Multiple example sentences with explanations]
I am going to show some [TARGET_STRUCTURE] sentences. You tell me if the [STRUCTURE_ELEMENT] I used is [OPTION_1] or [OPTION_2].
My turn. Listen. [PRACTICE_SENTENCE]. Get Ready. Go. (Children answer [CORRECT_ANSWER])
[Continue with practice examples and explanations]
B_model_explain_engage.example_output: Model target sentence structure with clear examples. Compare to previously learned structures. Use unit vocabulary in demonstration sentences. Explain purpose for genre writing.
B_model_explain_engage.reference: Form E for evidence-based vocabulary and sentence practices

C_guided_practice.explanation: The purpose of this section of the lesson is to guide children in applying the targeted sentence structure to express an idea that relates to topic and genre, incorporating their vocabulary words
teacher_script: Now you are going to do [GUIDED_ACTIVITY] +Level: Low. You are going to tell me information about [UNIT_TOPIC_ELEMENT]. You are thinking about [CONTENT_FOCUS]. You want to explain that [SENTENCE_PURPOSE].
I am going to give everybody a special [TARGET_STRUCTURE_ELEMENT]; the [STRUCTURE_CARD]. Everyone also has the [VOCABULARY_CARDS], along with your [GRAMMAR_ELEMENT_CARDS].
Look up here at our sight words. {Teacher draws children's attention to the sight word chart}
We know [SIGHT_WORD_EXPLANATION]. We also know that they can be capital or uppercase if we start a sentence, and lowercase if they do not start a sentence.

You are going to pick a subject. The subject of your sentence will be about one of these [SUBJECT_OPTIONS]. {Teacher displays pictures/options of different [SUBJECT_TYPE] children have learned about}.
You are going to create a sentence that shares information about [SENTENCE_CONTENT]. Watch me.
[Teacher demonstration with step-by-step modeling]
I picked the [EXAMPLE_SUBJECT]. I know that [BACKGROUND_KNOWLEDGE]. So I think [REASONING].
Let's look at our cards to build this sentence.
[Step-by-step sentence building process]
What do I need at the end of my sentence? (Children should answer 'period')
Right. So, I take my sticky note, and dot, for the period. Now everyone knows that is the end of my sentence. [COMPLETE_SENTENCE], period.
Now it's your turn. Everyone choose your topic, the [SUBJECT_TYPE] that is the subject of your sentence.
[Guided practice with individual support and examples]
C_guided_practice.example_output: Build-a-Sentence using cards and visual supports. Students create target structure sentences about unit topic. Teacher provides step-by-step guidance and individual support.
C_guided_practice.reference: Form D for alternative guided practice activities

D_application.explanation: The purpose of this section of the lesson is to provide children further practice using the new sentence structure to express their ideas and incorporate vocabulary from a unit of study
teacher_script: Alright everyone the last thing you are going to do is pick another [SUBJECT_TYPE] and create a [TARGET_STRUCTURE] sentence to tell me [SENTENCE_PURPOSE]. This time I want you to add one of our vocabulary words. We are doing the [APPLICATION_ACTIVITY] +Level Low.
After you create the sentence, choose a vocabulary word to describe the [DESCRIPTION_TARGET].
Look up here {Teacher directs children's attention to [VOCABULARY_DISPLAY]}
We have [VOCABULARY_WORD_1] and [VOCABULARY_WORD_2]. So you are thinking to yourself, How would I describe my [TARGET_ELEMENT]. Would it be [VOCABULARY_WORD_1] or [VOCABULARY_WORD_2].

To show me which word you chose, you are going to write either the letter [LETTER_1] for [SOUND_1] [VOCABULARY_WORD_1], or you will write the letter [LETTER_2] for [SOUND_2] [VOCABULARY_WORD_2]. You are writing that on your post it and adding that to your sentence. I am going to put five minutes on the clock. When I say stop, everyone puts their hands up. Get Ready. Go. {Teacher gives children five minutes to create their sentence, adding in an adjective vocabulary word. Teacher monitors to support students who may need extra support}.
Okay stop. Hands up. Hands down.
[Student name], tell us your sentence. (Child should respond: [EXAMPLE_STUDENT_SENTENCE]).

Why would a [SUBJECT_TYPE] be [VOCABULARY_WORD]? (Child should respond [REASONING]). Exactly, [EXPLANATION]. [VOCABULARY_DEFINITION]. [Additional explanation connecting to unit content]. {Teacher continues to take examples, writing them or displaying them for children to see, drawing attention to vocabulary and the [TARGET_STRUCTURE]}.
D_application.example_output: Add-A-Word challenge incorporating unit vocabulary into target sentence structure. Timed independent practice with teacher monitoring and support. Student sharing with explanations.
D_application.reference: Form D for alternative application activities

E_wrap_up.explanation: The purpose of this section is to remind children about the target structure, how it's different from previously learned structures and why they are important to the type of genre you are reading and writing in class
teacher_script: Everyone, we are working on writing [GENRE_TYPE], we want to [GENRE_PURPOSE]. [TARGET_STRUCTURE] sentences tell us [STRUCTURE_PURPOSE]. [CONTRASTING_STRUCTURE] sentences tell us [CONTRASTING_PURPOSE]. We need both kinds of sentences so that we can [COMBINED_PURPOSE].

I am going to give you a sentence, you tell me if it is [STRUCTURE_TYPE_1] –for a [STRUCTURE_TYPE_1] sentence or [STRUCTURE_TYPE_2] for a [STRUCTURE_TYPE_2] sentence. My turn. [EXAMPLE_SENTENCE_1]. Get Ready. Go. (Children should chorally respond [CORRECT_ANSWER_1]).
Very good. What special [STRUCTURE_ELEMENT] did I use? (Children should respond [STRUCTURE_ANSWER])
Excellent [STRUCTURE_ANSWER]. That is my [STRUCTURE_TYPE].
My turn. [EXAMPLE_SENTENCE_2] Get Ready. Go. (Children should answer [CORRECT_ANSWER_2]). Perfect! [EXPLANATION] is [ACTION_EXPLANATION]. It's an action. You all did awesome.
E_wrap_up.example_output: Compare target structure to previously learned structures. Explain importance for genre writing. Assessment through sentence identification. Reinforcement of learning objectives.

review_connect_activities.adaptation_prompt: Let me know if you would like activity examples, modifications of activities based on child ability level (low, middle, high)

low_level.name: Spotlight Sentence
low_level.description: Teacher reads or displays a sentence and asks, 'Who is this sentence about?' or 'What is happening?' Students identify the subject or verb aloud. 'Who did it?' and 'What did they do?'

low_level.name: Stretch It Out
low_level.description: The teacher shows a simple sentence. Children are given choices of the sentence structure they are reviewing and must add those sentence structures to the base sentence. For example, if focusing on delayed adjective phrases, children would choose either 'scared and lonely' or 'excited and happy' to add to the end of the base sentence: The cat shivered on the corner. This activity also integrates children's vocabulary building.

middle_level.name: Fix-It Fast
middle_level.description: Show or say a sentence with a missing part or jumbled order. Students help you quickly fix it together using previously learned sentence structures under review.

middle_level.name: The Missing Structure?
middle_level.description: Say or show a mix of sentences missing structures children previously learned (e.g., subjects, verbs, adjectives, prepositional phrases, etc). Students give a thumbs up if it's there, and thumbs down if it is not. Optional: Have children add in the structure if it's missing.

middle_level.name: Build and Say
middle_level.description: Give students word cards or visuals (subject, verb, object) and have them build a sentence and say it out loud. Keep it simple and quick.

middle_level.name: Silly Sentence Swap
middle_level.description: Read a sentence and swap one word to make it silly. Students tell you what part was changed (subject, verb, etc.).

middle_level.name: Act It Out Quick
middle_level.description: Read a sentence and have students act it out quickly, then review who did what to reinforce sentence parts.

high_level.name: Stretch and Repeat
high_level.description: Say a short sentence, and ask students to stretch it by adding one of the sentence structure parts they learned (e.g., an adjective or compound verb). Repeat a few times.

high_level.name: Sentence Snap
high_level.description: Flash a sentence for a few seconds. Remove it, then ask students what the sentence was about or to identify a key sentence structure part, like the verb or delayed adjective.

high_level.name: Paint Your Sentence
high_level.description: Children choose one of their vocabulary words, identify its part of speech, and correctly create and write a simple sentence using that word. The teacher then tells children they have a one minute challenge to add one more structure to their sentence (e.g., compound verb, prepositional phrase, adverb clause). (Kindergarten level or First Grade)

guided_practice_activities.adaptation_prompt: Let me know if you would like activity examples, modifications of activities based on child ability level (low, middle, high)

low_level.name: Same or Different
low_level.description: Teacher displays different types of sentences using previously learned sentence structures along with the targeted sentence structure. Children must listen to the sentence and identify whether the sentence includes the targeted structure (Same) or if it doesn't include the targeted structure (Different).

low_level.name: Sentence Hunt
low_level.description: Children are shown or read several sentences and must find the ones that match a specific sentence structure (e.g., subject + action verb).

middle_level.name: Build-A-Sentence
middle_level.description: Children are guided to create their own sentence by imitating a model (e.g., The whale is a ___). The teacher provides scaffolds such as visuals, word banks, or sentence frames to help children generate original content using a targeted sentence structure.

middle_level.name: Sentence Scrambler
middle_level.description: Children receive individual words or sentence parts (on cards or digital pieces) and must arrange them to form a complete sentence that matches a target structure.

middle_level.name: Stretchy Sentence
middle_level.description: Children start with a short base sentence (e.g., The dolphin dives) and are prompted to 'stretch' it by adding details using a specific structure (e.g., adding an adjective, prepositional phrase, or conjunction). The teacher may ask guiding questions like 'Where does the dolphin dive?' to support elaboration.

script: Great! Now we are going to play our Two Sentence Build-It Challenge +Level: High.

You are going to tell me information about a sea creature. You are thinking about whether that sea creature is a predator or prey. You want to explain that a particular sea creature is a predator or prey in their ocean habitat.
I am going to give everybody a special be-verb card; the 'is' card. Everyone also has the predator and prey card, along with your 'noun marker' cards, 'a' and 'the'.
Look up here at our sight words. {Teacher draws children's attention to the sight word chart}
We know 'the' and 'a' are words that come before a noun; they mark a noun. We also know that they can be capital or uppercase if we start a sentence, and lowercase if they do not start a sentence.
You are going to pick a subject. The subject of your sentence will be about one of these sea creatures. {Teacher displays pictures of different sea creatures children have learned about}.
You are going to create a sentence that shares information about whether your sea creature is a predator or prey. Watch me.
teacher_modeling: I picked the sea turtle. I know that sea turtles eat seaweed, and that bigger animals in the ocean, like the orca, can eat the sea turtle. So I think it is a prey.
Let's look at our cards to build this sentence.

So I am thinking: The sea turtle is a prey. First, I need to decide whether 'the' should be upper case or lowercase. It's starting my sentence, so I pick uppercase 'The.' I am going to place my uppercase 'The' card at the beginning. Then, I am going to put my sea creature, my subject –sea turtle– The sea turtle. Now I want to say something about the sea turtle, not what he does. So, I need my special be-verb card 'is'. My sea turtle is 'a' –I put my noun marker card next. And now I tell everyone what my sea turtle is –a prey. {The teacher reads the sentence back pointing to each card–'The sea turtle is a prey'}
What do I need at the end of my sentence? (Children should answer 'period')
Right. So, I take my sticky note, and dot, for the period. Now everyone knows that is the end of my sentence. The sea turtle is a prey, period.
guided_practice: Now it's your turn. Everyone choose your topic, the sea creature that is the subject of your sentence.
Everyone hold up your subject so I can see. (Children hold up a sea creature card that they have learned about.).
Find your noun marker card. Decide if you should use uppercase of lowercase 'the.'
Casey, what's your subject? (Child responds with 'the dolphin').
The dolphin.
Did you use your uppercase or lowercase card? (Child responds uppercase).
Right. You are starting a sentence, so you use uppercase. {Teacher takes one or two more examples}.
Alright, everyone check that you have uppercase 'The' in front of your sea creature. {Teacher checks}
So, what's next?
We want to say something about the sea creature.
What verb can do that? {Children should respond 'is'}.
Now tell me what your creature is: pick the the predator or prey card?
Make sure you mark your noun and use your sticky note for the period.
challenge_extension: Now challenge time. Take out your action verb cards for what predators do and what prey do. You are going to pick one action verb that your prey would do. Create another sentence with an action verb that shows what a predator or prey can do. So just place your action verb underneath your first sentence. You have 3 minutes. Get Ready. Go. (Children create an action sentence about their predator or prey)
Jasper, tell everyone what be-verb sentence you made. (Child responds, The walrus is a predator, period).
Perfect. Did the walrus do an action? (Child responds no)
So what kind of a verb did you use? (Child should respond 'be-verb').
Now Jasper tell us your action sentence. What does a walrus do that tells us that it is a predator? (Child should respond with something like the walrus hunts for fish in the ocean.
Perfect! 'Hunt' is something a predator would do, and we know that walruses do eat fish in order to survive. So they would be hunting.
{Teacher takes more examples, highlighting the difference purpose between the two verbs and relaying how one sentence is related to another to provide information to an audience}.

review_connect.explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to quickly review the type of text genre and content /unit topics children are learning and connect to the writing topic and purpose
teacher_script: [TEACHER NOTE: Ask teacher: 'What unit topic have you been studying?' and 'What texts have students been reading about this topic?']
Remember boys and girls we have been learning all about [UNIT_TOPIC].
What's a [KEY_CONCEPT] everyone? {Teacher points to picture cue of [KEY_CONCEPT]}
(Children respond, '[CONCEPT_DEFINITION].')
And [KEY_CONCEPT] gives [SUBJECT] what, everyone? {Teacher points to visual cues for [SUPPORTING_ELEMENTS]}.
(Children respond, '[SUPPORTING_ELEMENTS],' as teacher points to the cue).
Right, and we know that information because we've been reading some texts that give us information about [UNIT_TOPIC].
[Student name], what [SPECIFIC_FOCUS] are we learning about now? (Child responds, '[SPECIFIC_TOPIC]').
[Student name], [FOLLOW_UP_QUESTION]? (Child response: [EXPECTED_RESPONSE]).
Right, and we know that [ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT].
[Student name], how does that affect [CONNECTION_QUESTION]? (Child response: [STUDENT_INSIGHT]).
Exactly, remember our book? {Teacher references the text children have been reading}.
What [MAIN_SUBJECT] did we just get done reading about, everyone? (Response: [MAIN_SUBJECT_ANSWER]).

And we found out some cool information about the [MAIN_SUBJECT]. So today we want to share information about [MAIN_SUBJECT] and [WRITING_FOCUS]. We are writing [GENRE_TYPE]. So our topic is [MAIN_SUBJECT] and we want to focus on telling our readers all about [SPECIFIC_WRITING_PURPOSE]. [GUIDING_QUESTION]?
review_connect.example_output: Review unit topic and key concepts using visual cues. Connect to texts students have read. Establish writing purpose and guiding question for informational text.
review_connect.reference: Form E for evidence-based idea generation practices

model_explain_engage.explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is for the teacher to explicitly define the writing concept or skill and provide examples and non-examples so children clearly understand. Next, the skill or concept is directly modeled, step-by step so children can begin to apply the skill or concept during a writing task
teacher_script: The first thing we need to do is brainstorm. We need to remember the information we learned about [BRAINSTORM_FOCUS].
Here is our book. {Teacher displays book on overhead}.
We are going to do [TARGET_ACTIVITY] +Level = Middle about the information we learned that tells [ACTIVITY_PURPOSE].
{Teacher turns to page one.}
I am thinking about what I remember from this picture. I see [VISUAL_OBSERVATION]. That reminds me that we did read that [TEXT_CONNECTION].
Can anyone remember [RECALL_QUESTION]? [PROMPT_START] . . (Children respond: [STUDENT_RESPONSE]).
[CONCEPT_REINFORCEMENT].

So on my [TOOL_NAME], I am going to write [NOTE_CONTENT] in the first column under words. Remember notes are just words and phrases that help us remember the idea. So, I am going to write what I can. Then we'll draw next, but let's write we can first.

I know [PHONICS_EXAMPLE_1], begins with [LETTER_1], [SOUND_1]. And I know [WORD_2], [PHONICS_EXAMPLE_2] begins with [LETTER_2]. I also hear [SOUND_PATTERN], I hear [SOUND_DESCRIPTION], so I will write that. But now I want to sketch the picture. We are going to do that in this second column next to the words. It says picture at the top. And it doesn't have to be perfect, just a quick sketch. I am going to draw [DRAWING_DESCRIPTION]. [CONCEPT_CONNECTION].
This note helps me to remember what, [Student name]?
(Child response: [STUDENT_UNDERSTANDING]).
Exactly, so in my last column that says [COLUMN_HEADER], you see it says [FILL_IN_PROMPT]. We are going to fill in '[ANSWER]' as best we can by listening to the sounds we hear.
[Additional teaching and connections to deepen understanding]
Remember that is what we are trying to explain to our audience: [GUIDING_QUESTION]?
model_explain_engage.example_output: Model note-taking strategy using text and visuals. Demonstrate three-column approach: words, pictures, and how it helps. Use phonics skills for invented spelling. Connect to writing purpose.
model_explain_engage.reference: Form E for evidence-based idea generation and transcription practices

guided_practice.explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is for children to begin to apply the writing skill or concept during a task that is broken down into component steps so that children can practice step by step and have teacher feedback for improvement
teacher_script: Alright, now you are going to try to take a note on your [TOOL_NAME]. So the first thing you are going to do is look at the next picture. Everyone is going to think about what note they take. You are not saying it yet, you are thinking of that note in your head. When I say go, you are going to turn to your partner and share. Blue partner goes first, then green.
Get Ready, go ahead and think in your head. {Teacher waits a minute}.
Alright, turn to your partner. Blue Go. (Blue partner shares).
Stop. (Children turn back to the teacher).
Green Go. (Green partner shares).
Now that you shared, think of the final note you want to write about [NOTE_FOCUS].
{Teacher waits 20 seconds}.
[Student name], what is your note? (Child response: [STUDENT_NOTE_1])
[STUDENT_NOTE_1] (teacher writes down)
[Student name], what was your note? (Child response: [STUDENT_NOTE_2])
[Student name]? ([STUDENT_NOTE_3])
Great, all of these notes can help us remember. [EXPLANATION_OF_CONCEPT]. So you can write [NOTE_OPTIONS].
Everyone, take a minute and write what you can hear. (Children use invented spelling). {Teacher waits a minute or two and circulates to monitor progress}.
Great, our next step is to draw a picture. How do you think we could draw [DRAWING_CONCEPT]? {Teacher takes a few suggestions and demonstrates how to possibly draw the child suggestions.}
Okay, now you are going to draw your own, go ahead. {Teacher waits about a minute and circulates to monitor progress}.
The last thing we want to think about is [FINAL_QUESTION]?
Before you answer. Let me reread this sentence from the text. Listen.
[TEXT_QUOTE].
So what does it do? What verb did the text use, everyone? (Child response: [TEXT_VERB]).
Great so in the last column, it says [COLUMN_PROMPT], what? (Child response: [STUDENT_ANSWER]). {Teacher writes [STUDENT_ANSWER] in column three in the [TOOL_NAME]}.

guided_practice.reference: Form E for evidence-based transcription and idea development practices

application.explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to allow children practice in applying writing skills and concepts without the step by step guidance to check child facility with the writing process or task. The teacher can assess the degree to which the child has mastered the skill to further adapt instruction to child needs
teacher_script: Now you are going to do the next note by yourself. You are filling in the [ROW_NUMBER] row, and you are looking at page [PAGE_NUMBER] of your book. Everyone put a star next to the [ROW_NUMBER] row {Teacher demonstrates on the overhead–circulates to check students}.
Now open to page [PAGE_NUMBER]; I am coming around to check. Show me. {Teacher circulates to check}.
Remember our steps:
Think of the note.
Write a word or two as best you can.
Sketch the note
Fill in the blank about [FINAL_STEP_PURPOSE]. Remember you listen to sounds and write the word as best you can.
Okay. Go. {Teacher circulates as children write a note to monitor progress}.
Now you can share your note with your partner. Tell your partner the words you wrote, show your picture and tell how the note shows [SHARING_PURPOSE]. Green partner goes first this time.
Get ready. Go. {Teacher waits for a minute}.
Now Blue partner, go ahead and share your note. {Teacher waits for a minute}.
Who wants to share their note with the class? {Teacher allows a few children to share their notes, monitoring children's progress}.

So today we took notes that can help us write. Tomorrow we will talk more about how we can organize those notes in a way that makes sense to our readers.

*Let me know if you would like more examples to use in an activity or whether you would like me to increase or decrease the level of difficulty of an activity. Please specify whether the activity is in the Review & Connect, Model Explain Engage, Guided Practice, or Application part of the lesson.

review_connect_activities.note: All of these activities would be appropriate for all levels. The content of discussions and complexity of the skill will increase as children advance in their writing skills.

activities.name: Concept Picture Walk
activities.description: Children revisit key images from a shared text, anchor chart, or concept map. The teacher guides students to recall facts using questions like 'What do you see?' or 'What do you remember?' Children generate ideas by connecting pictures to unit concepts. This supports idea generation by activating background knowledge through visuals and guided discussion.

activities.name: Video Clip + Think-Pair-Share
activities.description: Children view a short video clip related to the unit topic and connected to texts being read (e.g., penguins in the cold). The teacher pauses to ask targeted questions that prompt children to think and talk with a partner. This helps them recall facts, build vocabulary, and connect new information to class learning.

activities.name: Genre Song or Chant
activities.description: Children sing a repetitive, upbeat chant set to the familiar melody of 'If You're Happy and You Know It.' For example, for informational writing, the chant could be:
example_chant: If it's real and it's true, it's a fact (clap, clap)
If it teaches something new, it's a fact (clap, clap)
And your facts are super plain,
Then you're working in the information lane! (clap, clap)
activities.visual_support: The teacher pairs the chant with visuals (e.g., a picture of a nonfiction book, animals, or diagrams) and gestures (e.g., pointing to the brain for 'think,' clapping for rhythm, miming writing or reading). This multisensory approach helps children internalize the purpose and structure of the genre through rhythm, movement, and repetition.

activities.name: Home-to-School Sharing Circle
activities.description: Children connect personal or family experiences to the topic of study (e.g., sharing what they wear in winter). The teacher helps children link these experiences to the genre and unit content (e.g., 'Just like you wear coats, penguins have feathers to stay warm.'). This builds relevance and supports idea development.

activities.name: Genre Poster Sort
activities.description: Children help sort sentence strips or images into categories (e.g., informational or narrative) based on what they learned about the features of each genre. This supports genre recognition and reinforces the kind of writing children will produce.

instructions: First explain or define in easy to understand terms the skill or concept
If appropriate, provide examples and non-examples of the concept
Explain and Engage means that the teacher provides explicit definitions and detailed examples to demonstrate a targeted skill

Examples are important and should be precise in demonstrating a concept or skill in order to dispel misconceptions. (e.g., what is and is not a topic sentence/ what is or is not a relevant detail) Use Engleman Theory of Learning and Form Z when providing examples and non-examples

engelmann_theory_application.concept: Cohesive devices link ideas and sentences so that writing flows and ideas connect logically

positive_examples.example: Penguins have thick feathers, so they stay warm in cold places.
Penguins swim fast, but they waddle on land.

model_explain_engage_activities.modeling_requirement: Model means for the teacher to demonstrate exactly what cognitive processes students must go through to complete a task or activity that builds a skill. The modeling should directly relate to what children are doing in their guided practice. Provide for teachers step by step modeling that is broken down by component steps steps.

guided_practice_activities.description: Guided practice has children engage in a cognitive process and use a particular skill or skills to complete a task in sequential chunks or steps that is monitored by the teacher. The teacher can provide feedback and the child can practice with teacher support. The teacher gradually intensifies what the child is doing by releasing control so that the child is doing more on their own until they can apply independently. A modification of any of these activities could be breaking down steps in smaller components for children who need more support or increasing the complexity of the task so that children are engaging with multiple components of the task at once for children who are advanced.

activities.name: Sentence Stem Topic Sentence
activities.description: Children are given a sentence starter (e.g., 'Penguins can survive the cold because...') and guided to complete it using information from shared readings or discussions. The teacher provides visual aids, oral rehearsal, and modeled responses to help children form complete topic sentences.

activities.name: Two Topic Sentences – Match the Details Level 1
activities.description: Children are shown two different topic sentences with clearly distinct subjects (e.g., 'Penguins' bodies help them survive in their habitat' and 'Tigers live in hot places like the jungle') along with three or four supporting details. With teacher guidance, children match the details to the correct topic sentence using images, shared reading content, or sorting cards.

activities.name: Two Topic Sentences – Match the Details Level 2
activities.description: Children are shown two topic sentences about the same subject but with different purposes (e.g., 'Penguins' bodies help them survive in the cold' and 'Penguins live in groups to stay safe') and are given three or four related supporting details. With teacher support, they determine which detail best fits each topic sentence by reasoning through the specific focus of each sentence.

activities.name: Two Topic Sentences – Match the Details Level 3
activities.description: Children are shown two closely related topic sentences (e.g., 'Penguins use teamwork to survive' and 'Penguins are built for life in the ocean') and are given four or more supporting details that require thoughtful sorting. With teacher prompting, children justify their matches using because-statements and generate an additional sentence that fits one of the topic sentences.

activities.name: Note-Taking of Relevant Textual Details
activities.description: Children revisit a shared text and write simple words to and draw representing pictures to take notes on key genre-specific details: Facts for informational text, Supporting details for opinion and response to reading texts, Problem and cause/effect of the problem for problem-solution texts, Steps or events for sequencing texts, Story events for narrative texts. The teacher provides visual support and models how to convert what they hear or see into simple notes.

activities.name: Relevant vs. Irrelevant Match Level 1
activities.description: Children are given a clear topic sentence (e.g., 'Penguins live in cold places') and four to six details. Some are clearly off-topic (e.g., 'Tigers live in the jungle'), and others are directly related (e.g., 'Penguins slide on their bellies over ice'). With teacher guidance and visual supports, children sort the details into relevant and irrelevant categories to reinforce paragraph unity using distinct and unrelated content.

activities.name: Circle the Cohesion – Words That Connect Level 1
activities.description: Children are presented with a short, teacher-written sentence pair or very simple paragraph using basic cohesive words (e.g., and, but, then). The teacher reads the text aloud with clear expression and models how these words help ideas stick together. Using a shared chart or sentence strip, the teacher prompts children to circle or highlight each cohesive word together as a group.

activities.name: Fact vs. Fantasy Level 1
activities.description: Children are shown two choices at a time—either through images, sentence cards, or oral storytelling. One option reflects a factual detail about a real-world animal, place, or process, and the other represents an imaginative or fantasy element. The teacher reads both aloud, then prompts: 'Which one could really happen in the world? Which one is just for fun or make-believe?' Children point, circle, or sort the correct choice with guidance.

activities.name: Fact vs. Opinion Level 1
activities.description: The teacher presents children with two simple sentences at a time—one factual and one opinion-based—paired with visuals and read aloud in a shared format. The teacher models the difference using sentence stems such as 'A fact is something that is true and can be proven' and 'An opinion is how someone feels or what they like.' Children are prompted to choose which sentence is the fact and which is the opinion.

principles: Application practice activities should be the same activity used in guided practice but the children do the task independently or apply the skill process to their own writing
For application, children either work with a partner/small group or they complete the task independently

Application activities can also be revised. For example, after doing the Build the Flow Level 3 task during guided practice, Students are given back their original writing pieces and asked to specifically revise for cohesive devices
revision_principles: Since revising is a new activity –teachers need to model the steps children are doing as the apply the skill/concept
Revising should always be focused on one specific skill as the regenerate an idea with genre in mind (organization) in early childhood
Revising is not Editing. When revising children should NOT be editing as well

Teachers can support struggling writers through revision processes in small groups. Teachers can provide prompts and scaffolds (word banks, sentence stems, visuals). Teachers can work with struggling students in small groups to help them apply but the application is more guided. More guidance means that the teacher has the child do one step, and checks it, then moves on to another step. To modify any activity, break the task down further into its component parts, according to theories of working and long-term memory. USE FORM Z for guidance

guided_practice_example.activity: Build the Flow – Rearranging for Cohesion Level 3: Fill the Gaps – Writing Cohesive Links
guided_practice_example.description: Children are given a paragraph with key cohesive elements missing. Some sentences are in the correct order, but the logical flow between them is unclear. Students are tasked with adding their own connecting phrases or transitional words (e.g., First, Then, Because of this, Although) in the blank spaces to improve cohesion.
guided_practice_example.example_text: The penguin is cold. ___________, it dives into the water to catch fish. ___________, it uses its wings to swim fast. It eats the fish quickly. ___________, it pops back up onto the ice.
guided_practice_example.student_response: The penguin is cold. Still, it dives into the water to catch fish. Then, it uses its wings to swim fast. It eats the fish quickly. After that, it pops back up onto the ice.

application_example.description: For application, children either work with a partner/small group or they complete the task independently. The teacher would give children a new paragraph with blanks and the child would do it himself. However, Application activities can also be revised. For example, after doing the Build the Flow Level 3 task during guided practice, Students are given back their original writing pieces and asked to specifically revise for cohesive devices.

teacher_script: We've been working on the [TARGET_SOUND] sound.
My turn. Listen to my sound [TARGET_SOUND].
Put your hand on your vocal box–now say the sound [TARGET_SOUND].
Did you feel your vocal box? (Children should respond based on voiced/voiceless sound)
That means you are using your voice, so we use our voice to make the [TARGET_SOUND] sound. (or adjust for voiceless sounds)
Where are your lips when you make the sound? (Children expected to say [LIP_POSITION]).
Right, [LIP_POSITION_DESCRIPTION].
And where is your tongue? (Children expected to say [TONGUE_POSITION]).
Yes, [TONGUE_POSITION_DESCRIPTION].
Let's do our sound motion. Get Ready Go. (children use [GESTURE_DESCRIPTION] while saying [TARGET_SOUND]. +Gesture: refer to Form G for gestures).
Let's try. My turn. [TARGET_SOUND]. [Student name], get ready. Go. (child pronounces sound)

{The teacher has each child in the group demonstrate the correct pronunciation and provides correction if necessary; if this is a whole group lesson, the teacher has all children repeat first. Then, the teacher will call on a few children who may need extra support}.

My turn. The word is [TARGET_WORD]. Get Ready...Go. (children should have lifted the card). Right. Everyone should have lifted the card because [TARGET_WORD] begins with [TARGET_SOUND]. Say it with me as you watch.
[STARTING_POSITION]. Say It. (children repeat).
[FIRST_STROKE_CUE]. Say it. (children repeat).
[SECOND_STROKE_CUE]. Say It (children repeat).
[THIRD_STROKE_CUE]. (children repeat).

Place your finger at the [STARTING_POSITION]. Let me see {teacher checks students finger placement} Remember it's important when we are writing to try to touch the lines. The lines are there to help us.
[LETTER_FORMATION_CUES with finger movements]
{Teacher has students do that a few times and repeat for lowercase [TARGET_LETTER]}.

(Children write using dotted lines as guides and say the sequence verbal cues: [LETTER_FORMATION_CUES])
Now you do one using the dotted lines. {Teacher monitors children's letter writing}.
Do one more using the dotted lines {Teacher monitors and repeats process for lowercase [TARGET_LETTER]}.

So I am thinking the beginning sound of '[EXAMPLE_WORD]' is [EXAMPLE_SOUND]. I know that the [EXAMPLE_SOUND] sound is written with the letter [EXAMPLE_LETTER]. I see letter [EXAMPLE_LETTER]. Now I am going to look to find letter [EXAMPLE_LETTER] on my paper. I am going to look at how to write the letter [EXAMPLE_LETTER]. Then, I am going to use the dotted lines to write the letter [EXAMPLE_LETTER].

Okay are you ready? Listen. My turn. The word is [TARGET_WORD]. Get ready. Go. (children should hear the sound [TARGET_SOUND] and write the letter [TARGET_LETTER]). {Teacher uses the same list of words that were used in the Sound Hunt activity above. *Let me know if you would like activity examples, modifications of activities based on child ability level (low, middle, high), or additional modeling.

Show me how to write it (children air write with sequence verbal cues: [LETTER_FORMATION_CUES])
Wonderful! Kiss your brains.

level_1_motor_foundation.name: Bumpy Road Letters
level_1_motor_foundation.description: Children trace textured letter cards (made from sandpaper or raised paint) with their fingers, following the correct stroke path by feel.

level_2_guided_formation.description: Children trace letters on dotted-line templates with a pencil, saying the strokes aloud.

level_2_guided_formation.description: Letters are printed with start dots and arrows. Children follow the marks to complete each letter step-by-step.

level_2_guided_formation.description: Children trace the same letter multiple times with different colored pencils, following correct formation for each layer.

level_3_semi_independent.name: Line Talkers
level_3_semi_independent.description: Children describe how the letter touches the lines.

level_3_semi_independent.name: Cover & Try
level_3_semi_independent.description: Children trace a letter, then cover the model and try writing it on their own, focusing on correct sequence and placement.

level_3_semi_independent.description: Children work in pairs—one child 'coaches' by checking if the other starts in the right place and follows the stroke order, using friendly reminders.

adaptation_4_activities.name: Trace the Sound You Hear
adaptation_4_activities.description: Teacher says a sound, but includes multiple opportunities for children to hear the target sound, and children trace the matching letter or letter pattern.

adaptation_4_activities.name: Write the Sound You Hear
adaptation_4_activities.description: Teacher says a sound, and children write the matching letter or letter pattern.

adaptation_4_activities.name: Sound-Letter Hunt
adaptation_4_activities.description: Teacher says words; children must listen to either the beginning, middle, or end sound to identify the target phoneme. Children then write the corresponding sound they hear.

adaptation_4_activities.name: Mystery Word Builder
adaptation_4_activities.description: Teacher gives sounds one at a time, and children write each sound as they hear it to form a word. Then they blend and read the completed word.

adaptation_4_activities.description: Children write a simple word, then change one sound when prompted to create a new word. Focus should be on the target letter-sound.

adaptation_4_activities.name: What's that Pattern
adaptation_4_activities.description: Teacher provides children with words that include previously learned sounds and the target sound. Children must segment the sounds in each word and write the corresponding letter or letter patterns.

form_e.title: Evidence-Based Practices
handwriting_spelling_practices: Teach the proper way to hold a pencil and write from left to right
Help children pronounce, identify, and isolate phonemes correctly
Teach how to form each letter representing a phoneme step by step, showing the exact order and direction of the strokes
Talk with children about how letters look—compare their shapes and the strokes used to write them
Have children retrieve prior phoneme-grapheme knowledge and connect to new phoneme-grapheme patterns
Cue children to apply phoneme-grapheme patterns during activities
Provide corrective and confirmatory feedback explaining what part is incorrect and showing them how to fix it
Encourage children to use what they've learned about sounds, spelling patterns, and word parts to try spelling new words—even if they're not sure (invented spelling)
vocabulary_sentence_practices: Provide multiple opportunities for children to use vocabulary words from their unit or theme during sentence generation tasks
Encourage children to play with words by making connections, grouping them into categories, and exploring how they relate to the writing topic or unit theme
Teach children connecting words like 'because' for cause and effect and 'also' to add ideas, helping them organize and link their thoughts clearly in writing
Explicitly and systematically focus on one language structure at a time—like subject-verb clauses or prepositional phrases–to build sentence awareness
Support children's sentence development by having them build, rearrange, combine, and expand sentences related to the writing topic or unit theme
Connect vocabulary to sentence writing by having children use words from a unit theme in sentences related to the writing topic
Prompt children to use specific vocabulary and sentence structures while they compose
idea_generation_practices: Clearly explain the writing topic and its purpose, and identify key features of the genre that support that purpose
Use visuals, read-alouds, and multimedia (like videos or photos) to help children learn about the unit topic, making it easier for them to talk and write about the topic
Help children connect the writing topic to what they've read, learned in the unit, or experienced in real life
Invite children to share their own experiences related to the topic—things they've seen, done, or talked about at school, home, or in their community

Model the brainstorming process by thinking out loud. Show children how to come up with ideas by saying your thoughts as you connect the writing topic to personal experiences, knowledge, or related vocabulary
Have young children draw their ideas before writing. This helps them clarify what they want to say and supports their working memory when turning ideas into written words
Use questions and prompts to help children expand their ideas, clarify their thinking, and revise their language before and during writing
Encourage children to orally rehearse their ideas by saying their complete 'crafted' sentence aloud before writing

They [ACTION]. So, the subject is [SUBJECT].

Let me show you some more examples. {Teacher displays example sentences, calling children's attention to the purpose of the sentence and the [TARGET_STRUCTURE] used for that purpose}.

I am going to show some [TARGET_STRUCTURE] sentences. You tell me if the [STRUCTURE_ELEMENT] I used is [OPTION_1] or [OPTION_2].

teacher_script: Now you are going to do [GUIDED_ACTIVITY] +Level: Low. You are going to tell me information about [UNIT_TOPIC_ELEMENT]. You are thinking about [CONTENT_FOCUS]. You want to explain that [SENTENCE_PURPOSE].
I am going to give everybody a special [TARGET_STRUCTURE_ELEMENT]; the [STRUCTURE_CARD]. Everyone also has the [VOCABULARY_CARDS], along with your [GRAMMAR_ELEMENT_CARDS].
Look up here at our sight words. {Teacher draws children's attention to the sight word chart}
We know [SIGHT_WORD_EXPLANATION]. We also know that they can be capital or uppercase if we start a sentence, and lowercase if they do not start a sentence.

You are going to pick a subject. The subject of your sentence will be about one of these [SUBJECT_OPTIONS]. {Teacher displays pictures/options of different [SUBJECT_TYPE] children have learned about}.
You are going to create a sentence that shares information about [SENTENCE_CONTENT]. Watch me.
[Teacher demonstration with step-by-step modeling]
I picked the [EXAMPLE_SUBJECT]. I know that [BACKGROUND_KNOWLEDGE]. So I think [REASONING].
Let's look at our cards to build this sentence.
[Step-by-step sentence building process]
What do I need at the end of my sentence? (Children should answer 'period')
Right. So, I take my sticky note, and dot, for the period. Now everyone knows that is the end of my sentence. [COMPLETE_SENTENCE], period.
Now it's your turn. Everyone choose your topic, the [SUBJECT_TYPE] that is the subject of your sentence.
[Guided practice with individual support and examples]

D_application.explanation: The purpose of this section of the lesson is to provide children further practice using the new sentence structure to express their ideas and incorporate vocabulary from a unit of study
teacher_script: Alright everyone the last thing you are going to do is pick another [SUBJECT_TYPE] and create a [TARGET_STRUCTURE] sentence to tell me [SENTENCE_PURPOSE]. This time I want you to add one of our vocabulary words. We are doing the [APPLICATION_ACTIVITY] +Level Low.
After you create the sentence, choose a vocabulary word to describe the [DESCRIPTION_TARGET].
Look up here {Teacher directs children's attention to [VOCABULARY_DISPLAY]}
We have [VOCABULARY_WORD_1] and [VOCABULARY_WORD_2]. So you are thinking to yourself, How would I describe my [TARGET_ELEMENT]. Would it be [VOCABULARY_WORD_1] or [VOCABULARY_WORD_2].

To show me which word you chose, you are going to write either the letter [LETTER_1] for [SOUND_1] [VOCABULARY_WORD_1], or you will write the letter [LETTER_2] for [SOUND_2] [VOCABULARY_WORD_2]. You are writing that on your post it and adding that to your sentence. I am going to put five minutes on the clock. When I say stop, everyone puts their hands up. Get Ready. Go. {Teacher gives children five minutes to create their sentence, adding in an adjective vocabulary word. Teacher monitors to support students who may need extra support}.
Okay stop. Hands up. Hands down.
[Student name], tell us your sentence. (Child should respond: [EXAMPLE_STUDENT_SENTENCE]).

Why would a [SUBJECT_TYPE] be [VOCABULARY_WORD]? (Child should respond [REASONING]). Exactly, [EXPLANATION]. [VOCABULARY_DEFINITION]. [Additional explanation connecting to unit content]. {Teacher continues to take examples, writing them or displaying them for children to see, drawing attention to vocabulary and the [TARGET_STRUCTURE]}.

E_wrap_up.explanation: The purpose of this section is to remind children about the target structure, how it's different from previously learned structures and why they are important to the type of genre you are reading and writing in class

I am going to give you a sentence, you tell me if it is [STRUCTURE_TYPE_1] –for a [STRUCTURE_TYPE_1] sentence or [STRUCTURE_TYPE_2] for a [STRUCTURE_TYPE_2] sentence. My turn. [EXAMPLE_SENTENCE_1]. Get Ready. Go. (Children should chorally respond [CORRECT_ANSWER_1]).
Very good. What special [STRUCTURE_ELEMENT] did I use? (Children should respond [STRUCTURE_ANSWER])
Excellent [STRUCTURE_ANSWER]. That is my [STRUCTURE_TYPE].
My turn. [EXAMPLE_SENTENCE_2] Get Ready. Go. (Children should answer [CORRECT_ANSWER_2]). Perfect! [EXPLANATION] is [ACTION_EXPLANATION]. It's an action. You all did awesome.

low_level.name: Spotlight Sentence

middle_level.description: Say or show a mix of sentences missing structures children previously learned (e.g., subjects, verbs, adjectives, prepositional phrases, etc). script: Great! Now we are going to play our Two Sentence Build-It Challenge +Level: High.

You are going to tell me information about a sea creature. You are thinking about whether that sea creature is a predator or prey. You want to explain that a particular sea creature is a predator or prey in their ocean habitat.
I am going to give everybody a special be-verb card; the 'is' card. Everyone also has the predator and prey card, along with your 'noun marker' cards, 'a' and 'the'.
Look up here at our sight words. {Teacher draws children's attention to the sight word chart}
We know 'the' and 'a' are words that come before a noun; they mark a noun. We also know that they can be capital or uppercase if we start a sentence, and lowercase if they do not start a sentence.
You are going to pick a subject. The subject of your sentence will be about one of these sea creatures. {Teacher displays pictures of different sea creatures children have learned about}.
You are going to create a sentence that shares information about whether your sea creature is a predator or prey. Watch me.
teacher_modeling: I picked the sea turtle. I know that sea turtles eat seaweed, and that bigger animals in the ocean, like the orca, can eat the sea turtle. So I think it is a prey.
Let's look at our cards to build this sentence.

So I am thinking: The sea turtle is a prey. First, I need to decide whether 'the' should be upper case or lowercase. It's starting my sentence, so I pick uppercase 'The.' I am going to place my uppercase 'The' card at the beginning. Then, I am going to put my sea creature, my subject –sea turtle– The sea turtle. Now I want to say something about the sea turtle, not what he does. So, I need my special be-verb card 'is'. My sea turtle is 'a' –I put my noun marker card next. And now I tell everyone what my sea turtle is –a prey. {The teacher reads the sentence back pointing to each card–'The sea turtle is a prey'}
What do I need at the end of my sentence? (Children should answer 'period')
Right. So, I take my sticky note, and dot, for the period. Now everyone knows that is the end of my sentence. The sea turtle is a prey, period.
guided_practice: Now it's your turn. Everyone choose your topic, the sea creature that is the subject of your sentence.
Everyone hold up your subject so I can see. (Children hold up a sea creature card that they have learned about.).
Find your noun marker card. Decide if you should use uppercase of lowercase 'the.'
Casey, what's your subject? (Child responds with 'the dolphin').
The dolphin.
Did you use your uppercase or lowercase card? (Child responds uppercase).
Right. You are starting a sentence, so you use uppercase. {Teacher takes one or two more examples}.
Alright, everyone check that you have uppercase 'The' in front of your sea creature. {Teacher checks}
So, what's next?
We want to say something about the sea creature.
What verb can do that? {Children should respond 'is'}.
Now tell me what your creature is: pick the the predator or prey card?
Make sure you mark your noun and use your sticky note for the period.
challenge_extension: Now challenge time. Take out your action verb cards for what predators do and what prey do. You are going to pick one action verb that your prey would do. Create another sentence with an action verb that shows what a predator or prey can do. So just place your action verb underneath your first sentence. You have 3 minutes. Get Ready. Go. (Children create an action sentence about their predator or prey)
Jasper, tell everyone what be-verb sentence you made. (Child responds, The walrus is a predator, period).
Perfect. Did the walrus do an action? (Child responds no)
So what kind of a verb did you use? (Child should respond 'be-verb').
Now Jasper tell us your action sentence. What does a walrus do that tells us that it is a predator? (Child should respond with something like the walrus hunts for fish in the ocean.
Perfect! 'Hunt' is something a predator would do, and we know that walruses do eat fish in order to survive. So they would be hunting.
{Teacher takes more examples, highlighting the difference purpose between the two verbs and relaying how one sentence is related to another to provide information to an audience}.

I am thinking about what I remember from this picture. I see [VISUAL_OBSERVATION]. That reminds me that we did read that [TEXT_CONNECTION].
Can anyone remember [RECALL_QUESTION]? [PROMPT_START] . . (Children respond: [STUDENT_RESPONSE]).
[CONCEPT_REINFORCEMENT].

So on my [TOOL_NAME], I am going to write [NOTE_CONTENT] in the first column under words. Remember notes are just words and phrases that help us remember the idea. So, I am going to write what I can. Then we'll draw next, but let's write we can first.

I know [PHONICS_EXAMPLE_1], begins with [LETTER_1], [SOUND_1]. And I know [WORD_2], [PHONICS_EXAMPLE_2] begins with [LETTER_2]. I also hear [SOUND_PATTERN], I hear [SOUND_DESCRIPTION], so I will write that. But now I want to sketch the picture. We are going to do that in this second column next to the words. It says picture at the top. And it doesn't have to be perfect, just a quick sketch. I am going to draw [DRAWING_DESCRIPTION]. [CONCEPT_CONNECTION].
This note helps me to remember what, [Student name]?
(Child response: [STUDENT_UNDERSTANDING]).
Exactly, so in my last column that says [COLUMN_HEADER], you see it says [FILL_IN_PROMPT]. We are going to fill in '[ANSWER]' as best we can by listening to the sounds we hear.
[Additional teaching and connections to deepen understanding]
Remember that is what we are trying to explain to our audience: [GUIDING_QUESTION]?
model_explain_engage.example_output: Model note-taking strategy using text and visuals. Demonstrate three-column approach: words, pictures, and how it helps. Use phonics skills for invented spelling. Connect to writing purpose.
model_explain_engage.reference: Form E for evidence-based idea generation and transcription practices

guided_practice.explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is for children to begin to apply the writing skill or concept during a task that is broken down into component steps so that children can practice step by step and have teacher feedback for improvement
teacher_script: Alright, now you are going to try to take a note on your [TOOL_NAME]. So the first thing you are going to do is look at the next picture. Everyone is going to think about what note they take. You are not saying it yet, you are thinking of that note in your head. When I say go, you are going to turn to your partner and share. Blue partner goes first, then green.
Get Ready, go ahead and think in your head. {Teacher waits a minute}.
Alright, turn to your partner. Blue Go. (Blue partner shares).
Stop. (Children turn back to the teacher).
Green Go. (Green partner shares).
Now that you shared, think of the final note you want to write about [NOTE_FOCUS].
{Teacher waits 20 seconds}.
[Student name], what is your note? (Child response: [STUDENT_NOTE_1])
[STUDENT_NOTE_1] (teacher writes down)
[Student name], what was your note? (Child response: [STUDENT_NOTE_2])
[Student name]? ([STUDENT_NOTE_3])
Great, all of these notes can help us remember. [EXPLANATION_OF_CONCEPT]. So you can write [NOTE_OPTIONS].
Everyone, take a minute and write what you can hear. (Children use invented spelling). {Teacher waits a minute or two and circulates to monitor progress}.
Great, our next step is to draw a picture. How do you think we could draw [DRAWING_CONCEPT]? {Teacher takes a few suggestions and demonstrates how to possibly draw the child suggestions.}
Okay, now you are going to draw your own, go ahead. {Teacher waits about a minute and circulates to monitor progress}.
The last thing we want to think about is [FINAL_QUESTION]?
Before you answer. Let me reread this sentence from the text. Listen.
[TEXT_QUOTE].
So what does it do? What verb did the text use, everyone? (Child response: [TEXT_VERB]).
Great so in the last column, it says [COLUMN_PROMPT], what? (Child response: [STUDENT_ANSWER]). {Teacher writes [STUDENT_ANSWER] in column three in the [TOOL_NAME]}.
guided_practice.example_output: Partner sharing and individual note-taking practice. Step-by-step guidance: think, write words, draw picture, explain how it helps. Teacher monitoring and feedback.
guided_practice.reference: Form E for evidence-based transcription and idea development practices

application.explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to allow children practice in applying writing skills and concepts without the step by step guidance to check child facility with the writing process or task. The teacher can assess the degree to which the child has mastered the skill to further adapt instruction to child needs
teacher_script: Now you are going to do the next note by yourself. You are filling in the [ROW_NUMBER] row, and you are looking at page [PAGE_NUMBER] of your book. Everyone put a star next to the [ROW_NUMBER] row {Teacher demonstrates on the overhead–circulates to check students}.
Now open to page [PAGE_NUMBER]; I am coming around to check. Show me. {Teacher circulates to check}.
Remember our steps:
Think of the note.
Write a word or two as best you can.
Sketch the note
Fill in the blank about [FINAL_STEP_PURPOSE]. Remember you listen to sounds and write the word as best you can.
Okay. Go. {Teacher circulates as children write a note to monitor progress}.
Now you can share your note with your partner. Tell your partner the words you wrote, show your picture and tell how the note shows [SHARING_PURPOSE]. Green partner goes first this time.
Get ready. Go. {Teacher waits for a minute}.
Now Blue partner, go ahead and share your note. {Teacher waits for a minute}.
Who wants to share their note with the class? {Teacher allows a few children to share their notes, monitoring children's progress}.
application.example_output: Independent note-taking practice using the same three-step process. Partner sharing to reinforce learning. Whole class sharing for assessment and celebration.
application.reference: Form E for evidence-based independent practice in idea generation

wrap_up.explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to remind children about the target writing skill or concept, how it's different or similar from previously learned writing skills or genre components, and why they are important to the type of genre you are writing in class
teacher_script: Everyone, we are working on writing [GENRE_TYPE], we want to [GENRE_PURPOSE]. The information we want to tell our audience is about [TOPIC_FOCUS] and [SPECIFIC_INFORMATION_GOAL]. So today we took notes that can help us write. Tomorrow we will talk more about how we can organize those notes in a way that makes sense to our readers.

*Let me know if you would like more examples to use in an activity or whether you would like me to increase or decrease the level of difficulty of an activity. Please specify whether the activity is in the Review & Connect, Model Explain Engage, Guided Practice, or Application part of the lesson.
wrap_up.example_output: Reinforce purpose of note-taking for informational writing. Connect to next lesson on organization. Remind students of genre goals and audience.
wrap_up.reference: Form E for evidence-based writing practices

P.title: Suggested Activities For Idea Generation & Organization

form_p.title: Suggested Activities For Idea Generation & Organization

review_connect_activities.note: All of these activities would be appropriate for all levels. The content of discussions and complexity of the skill will increase as children advance in their writing skills.

activities.name: Concept Picture Walk
activities.description: Children revisit key images from a shared text, anchor chart, or concept map. The teacher guides students to recall facts using questions like 'What do you see?' or 'What do you remember?' Children generate ideas by connecting pictures to unit concepts. This supports idea generation by activating background knowledge through visuals and guided discussion.

activities.name: Video Clip + Think-Pair-Share
activities.description: Children view a short video clip related to the unit topic and connected to texts being read (e.g., penguins in the cold). The teacher pauses to ask targeted questions that prompt children to think and talk with a partner. This helps them recall facts, build vocabulary, and connect new information to class learning.

activities.name: Genre Song or Chant
activities.description: Children sing a repetitive, upbeat chant set to the familiar melody of 'If You're Happy and You Know It.' For example, for informational writing, the chant could be:
example_chant: If it's real and it's true, it's a fact (clap, clap)
If it teaches something new, it's a fact (clap, clap)
And your facts are super plain,
Then you're working in the information lane! (clap, clap)
activities.visual_support: The teacher pairs the chant with visuals (e.g., a picture of a nonfiction book, animals, or diagrams) and gestures (e.g., pointing to the brain for 'think,' clapping for rhythm, miming writing or reading). This multisensory approach helps children internalize the purpose and structure of the genre through rhythm, movement, and repetition.

activities.name: Home-to-School Sharing Circle
activities.description: Children connect personal or family experiences to the topic of study (e.g., sharing what they wear in winter). The teacher helps children link these experiences to the genre and unit content (e.g., 'Just like you wear coats, penguins have feathers to stay warm.'). This builds relevance and supports idea development.

activities.name: Genre Poster Sort
activities.description: Children help sort sentence strips or images into categories (e.g., informational or narrative) based on what they learned about the features of each genre. This supports genre recognition and reinforces the kind of writing children will produce.

instructions: First explain or define in easy to understand terms the skill or concept
If appropriate, provide examples and non-examples of the concept
Explain and Engage means that the teacher provides explicit definitions and detailed examples to demonstrate a targeted skill

Examples are important and should be precise in demonstrating a concept or skill in order to dispel misconceptions. (e.g., what is and is not a topic sentence/ what is or is not a relevant detail) Use Engleman Theory of Learning and Form Z when providing examples and non-examples

engelmann_theory_application.concept: Cohesive devices link ideas and sentences so that writing flows and ideas connect logically

positive_examples.example: Penguins have thick feathers, so they stay warm in cold places.
Penguins swim fast, but they waddle on land.
positive_examples.explanation: Contrast is clearly marked with but

positive_examples.example: First, the penguin dives into the water. Then, it catches a fish.
positive_examples.explanation: Sequence is linked with first and then

positive_examples.example: Penguins have flippers. Also, they have webbed feet.
positive_examples.explanation: Additional information is added using also

negative_examples.example: Penguins have thick feathers. They stay warm in cold places.
negative_examples.explanation: No linking word; ideas are related but not explicitly connected

negative_examples.example: Penguins swim fast. They waddle on land.
negative_examples.explanation: Contrast is not made clear without a device like but or however

negative_examples.example: The penguin catches a fish. The penguin dives into the water.
negative_examples.explanation: The sequence is reversed and lacks words like first, then, or after to show order

negative_examples.example: Penguins have flippers. They live in the snow.
negative_examples.explanation: No clear connection between ideas; lacking a cohesive device that links function to habitat (e.g., because or so)

model_explain_engage_activities.modeling_requirement: Model means for the teacher to demonstrate exactly what cognitive processes students must go through to complete a task or activity that builds a skill. The modeling should directly relate to what children are doing in their guided practice. Provide for teachers step by step modeling that is broken down by component steps steps.

guided_practice_activities.description: Guided practice has children engage in a cognitive process and use a particular skill or skills to complete a task in sequential chunks or steps that is monitored by the teacher. The teacher can provide feedback and the child can practice with teacher support. The teacher gradually intensifies what the child is doing by releasing control so that the child is doing more on their own until they can apply independently. A modification of any of these activities could be breaking down steps in smaller components for children who need more support or increasing the complexity of the task so that children are engaging with multiple components of the task at once for children who are advanced.

activities.name: Sentence Stem Topic Sentence
activities.description: Children are given a sentence starter (e.g., 'Penguins can survive the cold because...') and guided to complete it using information from shared readings or discussions. The teacher provides visual aids, oral rehearsal, and modeled responses to help children form complete topic sentences.

activities.name: Two Topic Sentences – Match the Details Level 1
activities.description: Children are shown two different topic sentences with clearly distinct subjects (e.g., 'Penguins' bodies help them survive in their habitat' and 'Tigers live in hot places like the jungle') along with three or four supporting details. With teacher guidance, children match the details to the correct topic sentence using images, shared reading content, or sorting cards.

activities.name: Two Topic Sentences – Match the Details Level 2
activities.description: Children are shown two topic sentences about the same subject but with different purposes (e.g., 'Penguins' bodies help them survive in the cold' and 'Penguins live in groups to stay safe') and are given three or four related supporting details. With teacher support, they determine which detail best fits each topic sentence by reasoning through the specific focus of each sentence.

activities.name: Two Topic Sentences – Match the Details Level 3
activities.description: Children are shown two closely related topic sentences (e.g., 'Penguins use teamwork to survive' and 'Penguins are built for life in the ocean') and are given four or more supporting details that require thoughtful sorting. With teacher prompting, children justify their matches using because-statements and generate an additional sentence that fits one of the topic sentences.

activities.name: Note-Taking of Relevant Textual Details
activities.description: Children revisit a shared text and write simple words to and draw representing pictures to take notes on key genre-specific details: Facts for informational text, Supporting details for opinion and response to reading texts, Problem and cause/effect of the problem for problem-solution texts, Steps or events for sequencing texts, Story events for narrative texts. The teacher provides visual support and models how to convert what they hear or see into simple notes.

activities.name: Relevant vs. Irrelevant Match Level 1
activities.description: Children are given a clear topic sentence (e.g., 'Penguins live in cold places') and four to six details. Some are clearly off-topic (e.g., 'Tigers live in the jungle'), and others are directly related (e.g., 'Penguins slide on their bellies over ice'). With teacher guidance and visual supports, children sort the details into relevant and irrelevant categories to reinforce paragraph unity using distinct and unrelated content.

activities.name: Circle the Cohesion – Words That Connect Level 1
activities.description: Children are presented with a short, teacher-written sentence pair or very simple paragraph using basic cohesive words (e.g., and, but, then). The teacher reads the text aloud with clear expression and models how these words help ideas stick together. Using a shared chart or sentence strip, the teacher prompts children to circle or highlight each cohesive word together as a group.

activities.name: Fact vs. Fantasy Level 1
activities.description: Children are shown two choices at a time—either through images, sentence cards, or oral storytelling. One option reflects a factual detail about a real-world animal, place, or process, and the other represents an imaginative or fantasy element. The teacher reads both aloud, then prompts: 'Which one could really happen in the world? Which one is just for fun or make-believe?' Children point, circle, or sort the correct choice with guidance.

activities.name: Fact vs. Opinion Level 1
activities.description: The teacher presents children with two simple sentences at a time—one factual and one opinion-based—paired with visuals and read aloud in a shared format. The teacher models the difference using sentence stems such as 'A fact is something that is true and can be proven' and 'An opinion is how someone feels or what they like.' Children are prompted to choose which sentence is the fact and which is the opinion.

principles: Application practice activities should be the same activity used in guided practice but the children do the task independently or apply the skill process to their own writing
For application, children either work with a partner/small group or they complete the task independently

Application activities can also be revised. For example, after doing the Build the Flow Level 3 task during guided practice, Students are given back their original writing pieces and asked to specifically revise for cohesive devices
revision_principles: Since revising is a new activity –teachers need to model the steps children are doing as the apply the skill/concept
Revising should always be focused on one specific skill as the regenerate an idea with genre in mind (organization) in early childhood
Revising is not Editing. When revising children should NOT be editing as well

Teachers can support struggling writers through revision processes in small groups. Teachers can provide prompts and scaffolds (word banks, sentence stems, visuals). Teachers can work with struggling students in small groups to help them apply but the application is more guided. More guidance means that the teacher has the child do one step, and checks it, then moves on to another step. To modify any activity, break the task down further into its component parts, according to theories of working and long-term memory. USE FORM Z for guidance

guided_practice_example.activity: Build the Flow – Rearranging for Cohesion Level 3: Fill the Gaps – Writing Cohesive Links
guided_practice_example.description: Children are given a paragraph with key cohesive elements missing. Some sentences are in the correct order, but the logical flow between them is unclear. Students are tasked with adding their own connecting phrases or transitional words (e.g., First, Then, Because of this, Although) in the blank spaces to improve cohesion.
guided_practice_example.example_text: The penguin is cold. ___________, it dives into the water to catch fish. ___________, it uses its wings to swim fast. It eats the fish quickly. ___________, it pops back up onto the ice.
guided_practice_example.student_response: The penguin is cold. Still, it dives into the water to catch fish. Then, it uses its wings to swim fast. It eats the fish quickly. After that, it pops back up onto the ice.

application_example.description: For application, children either work with a partner/small group or they complete the task independently. The teacher would give children a new paragraph with blanks and the child would do it himself. However, Application activities can also be revised. For example, after doing the Build the Flow Level 3 task during guided practice, Students are given back their original writing pieces and asked to specifically revise for cohesive devices.
